Volume 05 · Chapter 03

Production, costs and firm choice

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v05-c02

By the endDerive cost functions and output/input choices from technology.

Choose a process, then choose an output

Capability: derive cost functions and output/input choices from technology. Prerequisite: demand, duality and welfare, especially minimization conditional on a target, together with constrained optimization. A workshop can choose its labor hours, rent machine services and decide whether to open. Producing a promised order cheaply and deciding whether that order is worth accepting are different problems. We solve them in that order, then connect their answers.

All technologies, prices and contracts in this chapter are original hypothetical examples. The firm takes both input and output prices as given, maximizes economic profit and knows its feasible technology. There are no taxes, externalities, uncertainty, financing constraints or adjustment delays beyond those explicitly specified. These are modeling assumptions, not conclusions drawn from observed businesses.

Technology, units and the feasible set

Fix one production day. Let q be units of finished output during that day, L labor-hours and K machine-service hours during the same day. The input prices w and r are USD per labor-hour and per machine-hour; p is USD per unit of output. Thus wL, rK and pq are USD for the day. K measures a service flow, not the purchase price or accounting book value of a machine. Numerical technology coefficients embody the conversion between these physical units. Continuous quantities are an approximation; an indivisible machine or output batch needs a discrete feasible set.

A single-output production function f(L,K) describes the maximum output attainable with those inputs. Its associated production set is T = {(L,K,q) ≥ 0: q ≤ f(L,K)}. In net-output notation a plan is y = (−L,−K,q), so its value at positive prices (w,r,p) is −wL − rK + pq. We use negative input quantities and positive prices consistently. A function is a convenient special representation: more general production sets can include multiple outputs, waste and alternative discrete processes.

Free disposal here means that increasing supplied inputs or reducing output preserves feasibility; monotone f supplies this property. It does not say that pollution disposal is socially free. An isoquant f(L,K) = q is a boundary for a specified output. Points with avoidable extra inputs are technically inefficient, but technical efficiency alone does not choose among different boundary points with different dollar costs. A concave f gives a convex T: a mixture of two plans can produce at least their mixed output. Setup requirements can destroy convexity, and we do not impose it universally.

At a smooth interior point, marginal products are MPL = ∂f/∂L and MPK = ∂f/∂K. They measure extra output per extra input unit while holding the other input fixed. Along a differentiable isoquant with MPK > 0, dK/dL = −MPL/MPK. We call the positive ratio MPL/MPK the marginal rate of technical substitution: machine-hours replaced by one more labor-hour locally.

Diminishing marginal product changes one input, holding the other fixed. Returns to scale change all inputs proportionally: for t > 1, compare f(tL,tK) with tf(L,K). Equality means constant returns; greater or smaller output means increasing or decreasing returns, respectively. For A LαKβ with positive exponents, scale output changes by tα+β, while labor's marginal product falls with L when α < 1. Thus diminishing marginal products can coexist with increasing returns to scale. Neither statement identifies a time trend in productivity.

For an official course route through production, marginal products and short-run costs, see the MIT 14.01 lecture summaries, sections 3.1–3.3. MIT identifies these as student-created summaries based on instructor Jonathan Gruber's lecture notes. The derivations below state the qualifications needed for corners, avoidable costs and nonattainment.

Conditional input choice and the cost function

For w,r > 0, define

C(w,r,q) = inf {wL + rK: L,K ≥ 0 and f(L,K) ≥ q}.

Assign C = +∞ if the requirement is infeasible. Conditional factor demand is the set of input pairs attaining this cost, conditional on output q. It is a correspondence when several pairs minimize; “the demand function” requires uniqueness. This problem has a specified positive target, so answering “use no inputs” is not generally feasible. If f(0,0) = 0 and q = 0, zero inputs minimize cost uniquely at strictly positive input prices.

There is a useful existence argument. Suppose the input requirement set is nonempty and closed. Pick a feasible pair of finite cost B. Any better pair belongs to 0 ≤ L ≤ B/w and 0 ≤ K ≤ B/r. Intersecting this compact rectangle with the closed requirement set gives a nonempty compact set, on which the continuous expenditure function attains its minimum. Inputs outside it cannot improve the answer. Strictly positive prices matter: with f(L,K) = LK, q = 1, w = 1 and r = 0, pairs (1/n,n) have cost 1/n, but no feasible pair costs zero. The infimum exists and the minimizing pair does not.

Where the target binds, inputs are positive, f is differentiable and constraint regularity holds, use ℒ = wL + rK + λ[q − f(L,K)], with λ ≥ 0. Interior stationarity gives w = λMPL and r = λMPK, hence MPL/MPK = w/r. Equal output per dollar is the local tangency condition. A concave technology and a feasible KKT tuple give a global certificate; alternatively prove optimality directly. Boundaries, kinks and nonconvexities require their own checks.

Cost has distinct properties in distinct arguments. Multiplying both input prices by a > 0 multiplies C by a and leaves the minimizing set unchanged. Increasing q shrinks the feasible set, so cost cannot fall. Cost is concave in input prices, because minimizing a weighted average of two expenditure functions gives a value at least as large as the same weighted average of their separate minima. By contrast, when f is concave, C is convex in output: mixing two minimizing input pairs produces at least the mixed output at their mixed cost. These properties are compatible; they concern different variables.

For an attained optimizer (L*,K*), a wage change δ gives C(w+δ,r,q) ≤ C(w,r,q) + δL*. Taking positive and negative δ shows that, if the cost derivative exists, ∂C/∂w = L*. Similarly ∂C/∂r = K*. This is the producer version of Shephard's lemma. At a price where the cost function has a kink, retain the optimizing set instead of selecting an arbitrary derivative. At a regular differentiable branch of binding output choices, the envelope relation gives ∂C/∂q = λ: the multiplier is marginal cost, in USD per output unit.

Scott Condie's author-hosted Theory of Supply notes, section 3.2, provide the production-set, conditional-demand and cost-duality definitions and a route to the general results. Here attainment is established before using an optimizer, and differentiability is stated before taking an envelope derivative.

Worked example 1: a flexible workshop and a committed machine

Let f(L,K) = 2√(LK), w = 9 and r = 4. For q > 0 the constraint is LK ≥ q²/4. The inequality between arithmetic and geometric means gives 9L + 4K ≥ 2√(36LK) ≥ 6q. Equality requires 9L = 4K and LK = q²/4, yielding

Lc = q/3,   Kc = 3q/4,   CLR(q) = 6q.

This proves global optimality and uniqueness without trusting a stationary point alone. At q = 12, use L = 4 and K = 9, spending 36 on each input, for cost 72 USD. More generally, at any w,r > 0 the same argument gives Lc = (q/2)√(r/w), Kc = (q/2)√(w/r) and C = q√(wr). Differentiating this C in input prices recovers those demands. The technology has constant returns to scale even though each marginal product falls as its own input grows with the other fixed.

Now the workshop has committed to K̄ = 9 machine-hours for the day and owes 36 USD whether or not it operates; no refund, resale or subletting is available. Only labor varies. Output q requires L = q²/36, so variable cost V(q) = q²/4 and total short-run cost is CSR(q;9) = 36 + q²/4, including at q = 0. The 36 is a common unavoidable cost of the day's alternatives.

For q > 0, MC = q/2, AVC = q/4 and AC = 36/q + q/4. AC reaches its minimum 6 at q = 12, where MC = AC. The long-run comparison is exact: CSR − CLR = (q − 12)²/4 ≥ 0. The selected plant is cost-minimizing at q = 12; at other outputs the opportunity to adjust K would help. This comparison includes the same machine-service price on both sides.

At output price p = 4, completing the square in pq − q²/4 − 36 gives the unique choice q = 8, L = 16/9. Revenue is 32, variable cost 16 and total profit −20 USD. Shutting down yields −36. Operating is better by 16 even though total profit is negative. The current choice cannot undo the machine commitment.

Short run, long run and the meaning of a fixed cost

The short run fixes at least one input or commitment; the long run permits all inputs in the stated technology to adjust. These are choice horizons, not universal calendar lengths. Holding K = K̄ gives CSR(w,r,q;K̄) = rK̄ + minL≥0{wL: f(L,K̄) ≥ q}. Allowing a choice of K gives CLR = infK≥0CSR. Therefore long-run cost is no higher at the same q under the same input prices and accounting of opportunities. A graph of the lower envelope need not touch every short-run curve at that curve's minimum average cost.

A fixed cost does not vary with positive output over the specified range. A sunk cost cannot be recovered or changed by the present decision. An opening fee payable only if production occurs is fixed over positive quantities yet avoidable by shutting down. A prepaid nonrefundable design bill is sunk. A payment owed under every current alternative is also irrelevant to their ranking, even if cash payment lies ahead. An owned machine that can be rented to someone else has an opportunity cost when used internally; its purchase history does not erase that alternative.

For a differentiable total cost, MC = dC/dq. For q > 0, AC = C/q; if C = S + V with constant S, then AVC = V/q and average fixed cost is S/q. All these averages and MC are USD per output unit, whereas C and S are USD for the day. Since dAC/dq = (MC − AC)/q, MC crosses AC at a differentiable interior stationary point of AC. It is a minimum only with the appropriate change from negative to positive derivative or another global argument. There is no theorem that every cost curve is U-shaped. With one variable input and positive MPL, dL/dq = 1/MPL, so MC = w/MPL; diminishing labor productivity raises this short-run MC.

Worked example 2: proportions, substitutes and a whole set of minimizers

A second process has f(L,K) = min{3L,2K}. At q = 12, feasibility requires L ≥ 4 and K ≥ 6. With w = 9 and r = 4, strict positivity of prices makes the unique cheapest pair (4,6), costing 60 USD. In general Lc = q/3, Kc = q/2 and C = (w/3 + r/2)q. The kink, rather than an interior marginal-product ratio, determines the mix.

Suppose instead the process is f(L,K) = 3L + 2K: either input can make the output. A unit made entirely with labor costs w/3, and one made entirely with capital costs r/2. At w = 9,r = 4, capital is cheaper, so the q = 12 order uses (L,K) = (0,6) and costs 24. At w = 6,r = 4, the unit costs tie at 2. Every nonnegative pair satisfying 3L + 2K = 12 minimizes; for instance (0,6), (2,3) and (4,0) all cost 24. Thus C = q min{w/3,r/2}, continuous but nondifferentiable in w at this tie for q > 0. No single conditional labor demand describes all optimal choices there.

Competitive supply is a global choice

Let Q(p) = arg maxq≥0{pq − C(q)} for a fixed technology and fixed input prices. This supply correspondence chooses output; the resulting input choices are the conditional demands at that output. A profit-maximizing plan must minimize the cost of its chosen output: replacing unnecessarily expensive inputs would raise profit without changing sales. Conversely, a global output maximum combined with cost-minimizing inputs gives a global plan maximum, provided these optima are attained.

At an interior differentiable optimum, p = MC. It is sufficient for the global output choice when C is convex on the feasible interval; strict convexity gives at most one optimum. At zero, at a capacity limit, or with operating fees and nonconvex costs, inspect the boundary and compare profits globally. Marginal revenue is p because the firm is a price taker. If its own quantity changes its selling price, differentiating revenue produces an additional term and this competitive rule does not apply.

Existence needs separate attention. A lower-semicontinuous cost on a compact output interval attains a profit maximum. Without a capacity bound, the sufficient growth condition C(q) − pq → +∞ as q → ∞ confines the optimum to a bounded interval. Smooth costs alone do not ensure it. For the flexible workshop's C = 6q, Q(p) = {0} for p < 6, all q ≥ 0 are optimal at p = 6, and profit is unbounded above for p > 6. The last case has no finite maximizing output. It signals that unlimited scaling, constant input prices and that output price cannot together describe a finite competitive firm equilibrium.

A useful supply comparison does not require differentiability or convexity. For attained choices q₁ at p₁ and q₂ at p₂ > p₁, optimality gives p₁q₁ − C(q₁) ≥ p₁q₂ − C(q₂) and p₂q₂ − C(q₂) ≥ p₂q₁ − C(q₁). Adding yields (p₂ − p₁)(q₂ − q₁) ≥ 0, hence q₂ ≥ q₁. This holds with ties and discrete quantities, provided the feasible set and costs stay fixed. A simultaneous wage, capacity or technology change prevents this particular cancellation.

Alexander Wolitzky's MIT 14.121 Lectures 6–7, slides 4–8 and 32, connect production choices with dual value functions and the law of supply. The two-inequality argument above is sufficient for this chapter; the later monotone-methods material is an extension.

Shutdown compares avoidable cost with revenue

Write the daily alternatives explicitly. Shutdown costs S. Operating at q > 0 costs S + F + V(q), where S is unavoidable now, F ≥ 0 is an avoidable opening fee and V(0) = 0. Relative to shutdown, operation gains pq − V(q) − F. Choose a positive quantity only if the best such gain is nonnegative; a zero gain gives a tie with shutdown. An already incurred sunk payment cancels from both alternatives.

If F = 0, the familiar shutdown comparison uses AVC = V(q)/q. More generally the relevant average avoidable cost is [F + V(q)]/q. Let its infimum over q > 0 be psd. Below psd, every positive output loses relative to shutdown; above it, some positive output beats shutdown, although a maximizer still needs to exist. At equality a positive-output tie exists only if that infimum is attained. In the workshop with V = q²/4, the infimum AVC is zero but no positive q attains it; at p = 0 only shutdown is optimal. The phrase “MC above minimum AVC” is shorthand requiring these qualifications and global optimality, not a universal supply formula.

Worked example 3: a fee creates a jump in supply

A separate workshop owes S = 30 USD regardless of opening. Its opening fee is F = 9, and V(q) = 2q + q² for q ≥ 0, in the same daily output and currency units. For p > 2, maximizing (p − 2)q − q² over positive q gives q̂ = (p − 2)/2. Its gain over shutdown is (p − 2)²/4 − 9. Alternatively, average avoidable cost 2 + q + 9/q has derivative 1 − 9/q² and unique minimum 8 at q = 3.

Consequently Q(p) = {0} for p < 8, Q(8) = {0,3}, and Q(p) = {(p − 2)/2} for p > 8. At p = 7 the positive stationary candidate 2.5 loses 2.75 USD relative to shutdown, so p = MC alone gives the wrong decision. At p = 10, produce 4: revenue 40, variable cost 24, opening fee 9 and unavoidable cost 30 give profit −23. Shutdown gives −30. If the fee were zero, every p > 2 would instead induce q = (p − 2)/2. Raising S alone changes reported profit, not this supply correspondence.

Exit changes the feasible commitments across a longer horizon; shutdown describes zero current output while specified commitments remain. If all future operating costs can be avoided, compare future revenues with all relevant future costs, including the opportunity cost of capital. Historical sunk losses do not become recoverable merely because we say “long run.” Dynamic exit with resale values, uncertainty or re-entry costs requires an intertemporal problem. This chapter supplies individual choices at given prices. Competitive equilibrium and surplus adds aggregation, market clearing, entry, tax incidence and surplus; individual first-order conditions alone do not establish market equilibrium.

Exercises

  1. For f = 2√(LK), calculate output, both marginal products and the positive technical-substitution ratio at (L,K) = (4,9). What happens if both inputs are multiplied by four? Then use g = L3/4K3/4 to show explicitly why diminishing own marginal products do not imply decreasing returns to scale.
  2. Derive the smooth workshop's conditional demands and C(w,r,q) for arbitrary positive prices by a global inequality. Evaluate them at q = 18,w = 16,r = 9, and verify both price derivatives of cost. At q = 12,r = 4, what happens to the input mix and cost when w rises from 9 to 36?
  3. For q = 15,w = 8,r = 6, solve cost minimization first for min{3L,2K}, then for 3L + 2K. For the substitute technology, replace r by 16/3 while holding w = 8. Describe the entire minimizing set, its cost, and why a tangency-only method is inadequate.
  4. Return to the committed K̄ = 9 workshop with w = 9,r = 4. At p = 5, find output, labor, revenue, variable/total cost, profit, shutdown profit, MC, AVC and AC. Compare its cost with long-run cost at the same output and explain the difference.
  5. For Worked example 3, give optimal output and profit at p = 7,8,10, retaining all ties. Now suppose the 9-USD opening fee has already been paid and cannot be recovered even if the workshop shuts. At p = 7, re-solve the decision and compare operating with shutdown profit, including both committed payments.
  6. Prove cost concavity in the vector of input prices without assuming a smooth production function. Separately show that, for fixed q and r and two strictly positive wages w₂ > w₁, any attained conditional labor choices satisfy L₂ ≤ L₁. State why neither proof by itself guarantees existence or a unique demand.
  7. For C(q) = 6q on q ≥ 0, describe supply at p = 5,6,7, first without capacity and then with q ≤ 20. As a distinct boundary case let C(q) = q − 1 + e−q and p = 1 on q ≥ 0. Establish that cost is nonnegative, increasing and convex, yet there is no profit-maximizing finite output. Identify the supremum and explain the failed existence condition.
  8. A manager uses Worked example 1 at p = 4 and adds an already paid nonrefundable 1,000-USD design bill to the −20-USD daily result. She proposes shutting today “to recover the loss,” calls her owned equipment free, and says the observed correlation of output with labor proves the technology. Evaluate these claims. For tomorrow only, the same K̄ = 9 service contract would cost an avoidable 36 USD, w and p would be unchanged, no other plant is available and there is no future strategic benefit. Should it be renewed? Give calculations and identify which facts must be verified for an actual business.
Complete solutions
  1. f = 12. MPL = √(K/L) = 3/2 and MPK = √(L/K) = 2/3, so their ratio is 9/4 machine-hours per labor-hour, equal to w/r in Worked example 1. Scaling both inputs by four gives (16,36) and output 48: constant returns. For g, gLL = −(3/16)L−5/4K3/4 < 0 for positive inputs, and similarly gKK < 0. Yet g(tL,tK) = t3/2g(L,K) > tg(L,K) for t > 1. At (1,1), each marginal product is 3/4 and each own second derivative is −3/16; doubling both inputs raises output from 1 to 2√2 > 2. Holding one input fixed and scaling both are different experiments.
  2. wL+rK ≥ 2√(wrLK) ≥ q√(wr), with equality exactly when wL=rK and LK=q²/4. Thus Lc=(q/2)√(r/w), Kc=(q/2)√(w/r), C=q√(wr). At (18,16,9), L=27/4, K=12, output 2√81=18 and expenditures 108+108=216 USD. Cost derivatives Cw=(q/2)√(r/w)=27/4 and Cr=(q/2)√(w/r)=12 have input-hour units. At q=12,r=4, increasing w from 9 to 36 halves L from 4 to 2, doubles K from 9 to 18, and raises cost from 72 to 144. The input ratio changes while LK=36 stays fixed.
  3. Fixed proportions require L≥5,K≥15/2; the unique optimum is (5,15/2), cost 40+45=85 USD. For substitutes, labor's unit cost 8/3 is below capital's 3, so (5,0) uniquely minimizes at cost 40. At r=16/3, both unit costs are 8/3. All pairs L∈[0,5], K=(15−3L)/2 minimize, each costing 40. The first technology uses a kink, the second a corner, and the equal-unit-cost case an entire segment; a smooth interior tangency cannot distinguish these regimes.
  4. Maximizing 5q−q²/4−36 gives q=10 and L=100/36=25/9. Revenue is 50, variable cost 25, total cost 61 and profit −11; shutdown gives −36. The gain from operating is 25. MC=5, AVC=5/2 and AC=61/10 USD per unit. Long-run cost at q=10 is 60, attained with L=10/3,K=15/2. The committed plant costs one extra dollar: (10−12)²/4=1. Long-run flexibility changes the feasible input mix; it does not erase an existing commitment retrospectively.
  5. At p=7 choose q=0 and profit −30; the q=5/2 candidate's incremental gain is 25/4−9=−11/4. At p=8, q=0 and q=3 both yield −30. At p=10, q=4 gives profit −23. Once the 9 is genuinely unavoidable, combined committed costs are 39 and incremental gain is (p−2)q−q². At p=7, q=5/2 yields contribution 25/4 and profit 25/4−39=−131/4=−32.75; shutdown gives −39. Produce. The ranking changes because the available refund/payment alternatives changed, not because renaming a cost changes its economic substance.
  6. Write a=(w,r), let Z(q) be the common feasible input set and let θ∈[0,1]. Every z∈Z(q) satisfies [θa+(1−θ)b]·z ≥ θC(a,q)+(1−θ)C(b,q). Taking its infimum proves C(θa+(1−θ)b,q) ≥ θC(a,q)+(1−θ)C(b,q), for finite costs; attainment is unnecessary. For attained choices at two wages, w₁L₁+rK₁≤w₁L₂+rK₂ and w₂L₂+rK₂≤w₂L₁+rK₁. Adding and rearranging gives (w₂−w₁)(L₂−L₁)≤0, hence L₂≤L₁. Fixed q and r keep the feasible set and remaining prices common. These are value and comparison inequalities; they do not supply compactness, attainment or strict preferences among input bundles. The substitute tie gives nonunique demand, while the zero-price example illustrates nonattainment outside the positive-price existence conditions.
  7. Without capacity: at p=5, profit −q gives Q={0}; at p=6, all q≥0 give zero profit; at p=7, profit q is unbounded and Q is empty. With q≤20, the respective sets are {0}, [0,20], {20}; the last maximum profit is 20 USD. For the second cost, C(0)=0, C′=1−e−q≥0 and C″=e−q>0, so it is nonnegative and strictly convex. Profit at p=1 is 1−e−q, strictly increasing toward 1 USD and below 1 at every finite q. The supremum is finite but unattained. The feasible set is unbounded and C(q)−pq=−1+e−q does not tend to +∞. This does not contradict compact-set existence or strict-convexity uniqueness conditional on existence.
  8. Today's operating profit is −20 versus −36 when shut. A cumulative comparison including the historical design bill gives −20−1,000=−1,020 versus −36−1,000=−1,036; this subtraction does not turn the historical bill into today's incremental cost. Operation improves either comparison by 16, and neither choice recovers the design bill. Owned equipment may forgo rental income or resale value; ownership alone does not imply zero opportunity cost. A labor/output correlation may reflect chosen inputs, demand, capital and productivity differences; it does not identify f or the causal effect of changing labor. Tomorrow, if the only productive option is the same contract, the best operating choice remains q=8 with contribution 16, less than its avoidable 36: profit −20 versus zero without renewal. Do not renew under the stated one-day alternatives. A sound real recommendation checks demand/price-taking, attainable output and quality, wages and hours, cancellation and rental/resale rights, all incremental costs, and future commitments or benefits. Credit requires both numerical comparisons, correct timing/opportunity-cost reasoning and an explicit identification limit; an unsupported universal closure recommendation is insufficient.

Teach-back and Delayed check

Teach-back: explain to a manager why an input can be fixed, a payment can be avoidable, and negative total profit can coexist with a rational decision to operate. Derive one conditional cost function, then explain exactly which extra assumptions turn its derivative into a competitive supply rule.

Delayed check: without looking back, solve the smooth technology at q=12,w=16,r=4. Then find the opening decision in Worked example 3 at p=15/2. Give an example of multiple optimal quantities and an example of no finite optimizer.

Delayed-check targets

The input choice is L=3,K=12 and cost 96; both input expenditures are 48. In the fee example the positive candidate is q=11/4, but gain over shutdown is 121/16−9=−23/16, so choose zero. C=6q at p=6 gives every nonnegative quantity as an optimum; at p=7 without capacity profit is unbounded, while Exercise 7's exponential example has a finite unattained supremum.

Sources and next steps

The linked MIT and author-hosted notes support the stated method routes; the workshop technologies, contract comparisons, numerical exercises and proofs are developed here. The checker independently verifies their arithmetic and selected boundary cases; finite calculations do not establish empirical technology or replace the written existence arguments. Graduate production duality, multi-output technologies and dynamic investment belong to later volumes. Continue from consumer duality to this firm's choices, then to competitive equilibrium and surplus.

Sources and further study

  • MIT 14.01 Principles of Microeconomics, Fall 2023 — Student-created Full Lecture Summaries based on Jonathan Gruber's lecture notes, sections 3.1–3.3 — Official university course resource for production functions, marginal products, returns to scale, conditional cost minimization, short-run/long-run costs and competitive shutdown. These are student-created summaries of the instructor's notes. Original examples and qualified derivations are supplied in the chapter.
  • Scott Condie — Advanced Microeconomic Theory Class Notes, Chapter 3: The Theory of Supply, section 3.2 — Author-hosted teaching source for production sets/free disposal, supply and conditional-factor-demand correspondences, cost homogeneity/price concavity, Shephard's lemma and output convexity under concave technology.
  • Alexander Wolitzky — MIT 14.121 Lectures 6–7: Monotone Comparative Statics, with Applications to Producer Theory, Fall 2015 — Primary university route for price-taking production-plan optimization, producer/consumer value-function analogies and the law of supply beyond smooth first-order conditions.
